chapter_theme: The lament turns to death and return (the lamp that goes out, the release not had in eight hundred yugas) and to the marks of the Saiva: white ash, Siva's guise, service to his servants, the light on the hill that Vishnu as a boar could not find. Then the body is run through its figures of contempt, puppet, nine-stringed house, worm-nest, salt-pot, rice-bag, a thing to be thrown off, and the run ends with the great secret the four Vedas cried for and did not see, and the darkness of every birth from grass to man.
structure_note: Chaining is looser than in the first run; instead the stanzas group: death and the guru (26 to 27), the Saiva marks (28 to 31), doctrine and absorption (32 to 35), the belly and its wants (36 to 38), the body as puppet and vessel (39 to 47), and the close on the net, the secret and the births (48 to 50). சூத்திரம் runs through 39 and 40 as puppet-string and as formula.

26.reading: Like darkness closing in as soon as a lit lamp goes out, when shall I learn the way I died and came back alive?
26.nuance: The lamp going out is death, the darkness that follows the interval, and வந்த the return into a body; the stanza asks to know the mechanism of rebirth (வகை), not to escape it yet. மாண்டு பிழைத்து can also be 'nearly dying and surviving', but the rebirth sense fits the chain into 28.

27.reading: Without my mind whirling and withering like a fish in a creel, when shall I seek out the noble one and bow at his feet?
27.nuance: தூரி is the fisherman's basket; the fish in it is caught and still thrashing. ஆரியன், the noble one, is taken by tradition as the guru, and the bowing at the feet fits that; it is also an epithet of Siva.

28.reading: To gain the release not reached in eight hundred yugas, when shall I shine wearing the white ash?
28.nuance: The stanza gives the ash as the means to release, with no inner reading attached; எண்ணூறு யுகம் is a round number for all the past births. It sits oddly beside 17, which denies that stone and copper can be the Real, and beside Sivavakkiyar's question what the ash is for.

29.reading: Not wandering here wearing a false guise, when shall I excel wearing the guise of Siva?
29.nuance: அவவேடம் is Tirumular's word for the ascetic's dress worn without the life. சிவவேடம் can be the true Saiva emblems or the form of Siva taken on within; the stanza keeps வேடம் for both and so does not say whether the true guise is still a guise.

30.reading: When shall I serve as a servant to the servants of Siva, who drank the poison for the gods and dances in the hall?
30.nuance: Two acts name the Lord: the poison drunk for others and the dance at Chidambaram. The service asked is at one remove, to the devotees, the தொண்டருக்குத் தொண்டன் of the bhakti tradition rather than the Siddhars' usual solitary line.

31.reading: When shall I tell of the lamp's light on the hill, which Vishnu did not find though he took the form of a boar and dug up the earth?
31.nuance: The story is Siva as the column of fire, Vishnu digging as a boar for its foot and Brahma flying for its crown; the hill is Annamalai, where the flame is lit as a lamp (தீபம்). The stanza gives the light to the one who can only tell of it, not to the god who dug.

32.reading: The sweet clear nectar, the inner meaning of Siddhanta, the seed of release: when shall I think of it first of all?
32.nuance: Three names for one thing. The nectar is the Siddhars' inner nectar or the sweetness of the teaching; உட்பொருள் makes the Siddhanta a text with a hidden sense; முதல் நினைப்பது, thinking of it first, puts it before everything else that is thought.

33.reading: Leaving behind all of Vedanta and the Veda, when shall I now stay alone in absorption?
33.nuance: நிட்டை (nishta) is the absorbed state and ஏகாந்தம் solitude in it. The leaving is of all scripture (எல்லாம்), without the usual distinction between the Veda's rites and its end; whether the texts are discarded or finished with is not said.

34.reading: Not spending the days of my life seeking some other place, when shall I seek the place that is reached and sleep there?
34.nuance: மற்றிடம் against உற்றிடம்: the place elsewhere against the place one is already at or that is fitting, read by the Siddhars as the body or the heart. உறங்குவது is again the sleep of 2 and 3.

35.reading: When shall I know the way those of the hall say that it is false that those here today will be here tomorrow?
35.nuance: மன்றுளோர் may be the men of the assembly, the wise, or the one in the hall of the dance; the saying itself is the plain stuff of the impermanence chapters. The ask is not to be told it but to know it in their way (வகை).

36.reading: Not drinking ganja, opium and toddy and withering, when shall I drink the five-fold nectar?
36.nuance: பஞ்சாமிர்தம் is the offering of five sweet things poured over the image; the Siddhars also read it as the nectar within. The three intoxicants are those Sivavakkiyar names as the fraud-yogis' habit, and the contrast is between two things drunk.

37.reading: To gain the release in this birth that gathered through the red waters, when shall I leave agitation and reach your refuge?
37.nuance: செஞ்சலம் (red water) and சஞ்சலம் (agitation) are a sound-pair. The red water is taken as the blood of the womb from which the body gathered (திரண்ட), so that the body born of blood is the one in which release (சென்ன மோட்சம், release in this janma) is to be had; the syntax is loose and I can't fix what திரண்ட modifies.

38.reading: Seeking food for the belly in every place where someone will give it, when shall I now stop this fretful wandering?
38.nuance: கும்பி is the belly as a pot. The stanza is against the renouncer's own begging round, not against householders' giving; the fault is வெம்பித் திரிகை, roaming in distress for food.

39.reading: Wandering until the dancing thread is cut, when shall I praise you before the day comes on which this thing is thrown away?
39.nuance: ஆடுகின்ற சூத்திரம், the thread that dances, is the string of the puppet of the body, cut at death; போடுகின்ற நாள் is the day the corpse is put out. சூத்திரம் then changes sense in 40.

40.reading: Not wandering about calling the house of nine threads 'I', when shall I discern and know the thread of Siva?
40.nuance: நவசூத்திர வீடு is the body: a house with nine strings (the puppet of 39) or nine openings, the nine gates. சிவசூத்திரம் is then the formula or working of Siva, as tradition takes it, the secret of 16 in Siva's name; the pun on சூத்திரம் as string and as sutra carries the sense and cannot be resolved into one.

41.reading: Leaving the worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow and spread, when shall I stand hidden and merged beneath your twin feet?
41.nuance: புழுக்கூடு, the nest of worms, is a stock Siddhar and Thiruppugazh name for the body; the stanza sets the flowing filth against the feet as two places to stand.

42.reading: Throwing down this puppet that I took up as a sinner in this life to match the two karmas, when shall I stand praising you?
42.nuance: இருவினைக்கு ஈடாய், as the equivalent of the two deeds, makes the body the exact payment for good and bad karma; பொம்மை, doll or puppet, keeps the string of 39. The body is thrown down (போட்டு) before praise, not after.

43.reading: Before this salted pot breaks and takes a womb again, when shall I become the subject of the Lord whose matted hair holds the water?
43.nuance: உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம், a pot that has had salt put in it, is the body: salt-cured and keeping, yet a clay pot that breaks. அப்பிட்ட வேணியன் answers it with the water (அப்பு, the Ganga) put in Siva's hair; the two இட்ட set the brittle salt-pot against the one who holds the river.

44.reading: Doing service and seeing the vision of Siva's form, when shall I shed the puppet and gain the fruit?
44.nuance: பாவை is the doll or image, here the body, as பொம்மை in 42; the service and the vision come before it is shed, so the body is used up rather than refused.

45.reading: Like the dark cloud that drew up water and went back, when shall I set the pot aside and reach the Supreme?
45.nuance: காண்டம் is taken as water (a lexicon sense), so the cloud takes water from the sea and returns to the sky; it could also be a portion or a section of a text. பாண்டம், the pot, is the body of 43. The simile's point seems to be a return to the source after a taking, but the first line cannot be fixed.

46.reading: Not carrying this leather bag of rice about and withering, when shall I throw off the filthy inert body and reach you?
46.nuance: துருத்தி is a leather water-bag; filled with cooked rice it is the body, a skin full of food. சடம், the inert thing, is the body as mere matter, set against உனை, the one reached.

47.reading: Not carrying the bond as if it were lasting and withering under it, when shall I strip off the garment of the body and know you?
47.nuance: தொடக்கு is a bond or fetter and சதம் permanence or a hundred; 'carrying the fetter as a hundred' may mean taking it for lasting, or for wealth. உடக்கை is read as உடுக்கை, clothing, so the body is a garment to be removed (கழற்றி), as the pot and the bag were in 43 and 46.

48.reading: Not caught and perishing in the bond of desire's net, when shall I stand joined in the lamp of the sounding bell?
48.nuance: ஓசைமணித் தீபம் joins sound (ஓசை, the bell மணி) and light in one object; tradition reads it as nada and jyoti, the sound and light met within at the crown. The plain image is a lamp that rings, and the stanza asks to be joined in it (ஒன்றி), not to see it.

49.reading: When shall I look upon the great secret that the four rare Vedas called out for and did not see?
49.nuance: கூப்பிட்டும் காணாத, cried out for and still did not see: the Vedas are not false but are left outside, calling. பார ரகசியம், the great or heavy secret, is what 33 left the Vedas for.

50.reading: As grass, as beast, as worm, as the form of a man: when shall the darkness of every birth depart?
50.nuance: The ascending list of births is the one Manikkavasagar's Sivapuranam opens with (புல்லாகி பூடாய்), compressed to four; இருள், darkness, is what all of them share, not any one of them.

links.note: Both make death a lamp put out: Tirumular's flame is taken while the bowl remains and the fools cry over the bowl; Pattiragiriyar's lit lamp goes out and darkness closes in at once, and he asks to learn the way he died and came back. Tirumular's lamp ends in the mourners' ignorance, Pattiragiriyar's in a question about return.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after it; Pattiragiriyar asks to know the way (வகை) by which he died and came back alive, as darkness follows a lamp going out. Both treat death and the next birth as one continuous passage, and Pattiragiriyar wants the passage itself understood.

Arunagiri is caught in the sorrowful household like a fish in a net (சமுசார வலை மீன்); Pattiragiriyar's mind whirls like a fish in a creel (தூரியினில் மீன்). The trapped fish is the self in the world in both, and in both the way out is the feet, the guru's in Pattiragiriyar and Murugan's in Arunagiri.

Tirumular: those who wear the holy ash without letting it fade will find deeds gone, the Siva state come and the holy feet reached; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will shine wearing the white ash so as to gain the release not had in eight hundred yugas. Both give the ash itself a place on the way to release.

Sivavakkiyar asks those born and dead in every birth what this ash is that they smear on, and says clarity comes only if they cut off impurity and desire along with the water; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will shine wearing the white ash so as to gain the release missed in eight hundred yugas. The conflict holds if 28 credits the ash with the release; if the ash is only the Saiva's mark worn on the way, as 29's சிவவேடம் suggests, Sivavakkiyar's question still stands but is not denied.

Tirumular's chapter on false guise (அவவேடம்) says fools who put on guises to frighten people into feeding them will not see Siva's feet however they dance and weep; Pattiragiriyar uses the chapter's word, அவவேடம், for the guise he wants to stop wandering in. Both treat the garb worn for a living as the opposite of the Saiva's dress.

Tirumular says the pure Saivas are those who go beyond garb (வேடம் கடந்து) and reach Siva without show; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will excel wearing Siva's garb (சிவவேடம் பூண்டு). The conflict holds if சிவவேடம் is the outward Saiva emblems, which 1438 sets aside; if it means taking on Siva's own form within, the two say the same thing in different words.

Both name Siva by the poison drunk so that others could have nectar: Tirumular's exalted one who drank the poison so the great might drink nectar, Pattiragiriyar's Siva who drank poison for the gods and dances in the hall. Tirumular makes him the giver of knowledge by the path of tapas; Pattiragiriyar asks only to serve his servants.

Tirumular tells the story straight: Brahma and Vishnu sought foot and crown and did not see his form, and Brahma lied. Pattiragiriyar keeps Vishnu's boar digging the earth and not seeing (மால்காணா), sets the light on the hill, and asks when he will be the one to tell of it. Both make the gods' failure the measure of the light.

Tirumular says Vedanta is where craving ends, and those who have truly heard it have let craving go; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will leave behind all of Vedanta and the Veda (வேதாந்தவேதம் எல்லாம் விட்டொழிந்தே) and stay alone in absorption. The conflict holds if 33 discards Vedanta as a teaching; if it means leaving the texts once their hearing has done its work, the two agree, and 229's 'hearing that leaves craving' is exactly what 33 leaves.

Sivavakkiyar calls those who say 'far, far' lazy and those who run through town, country and forest searching mutes, since the Supreme is spread everywhere; Pattiragiriyar asks not to spend his days seeking some other place (மற்றிடம்) but to seek the place already reached (உற்றிடம்) and sleep there. Both put the search close rather than far, and Pattiragiriyar adds that the finding is a sleep.

Sivavakkiyar's frauds, who pose as eaters of kaya-kalpa, smoke ganja at set hours and eat opium and roam the land like dogs; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stop drinking ganja, opium and toddy and drink the five-fold nectar instead. The same three drugs are the yogi's false intoxication in both, and Pattiragiriyar sets the true drink against them.

Sivavakkiyar's oxen in ochre and matted hair leave their wives to drift, roam every land and beg for crumbs at every house; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stop fretting from place to place after whoever will give food for the belly. Both see the renouncer's begging round as a wandering for the stomach, not for the Lord.

Tirumular's Lord set the body with nine gates as sluices (மடைவைத்த ஒன்பது வாய்தல்) and the fire in the lotus of the head, and the poet joins hands with him for it; Pattiragiriyar's nine-threaded house (நவசூத்திர வீடு) is the thing he must stop calling 'I' in order to know Siva's thread. The nine-fold body is the maker's work in one and the ego's error in the other.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot seeping filth from nine openings, which the fool addresses in the words of love poetry; Pattiragiriyar's is a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow and spread. The Naladiyar uses the image against desire for another's body, Pattiragiriyar against attachment to his own, and sets the feet against it.

Tirumular's Lord makes the elements dance like the deed that makes a false puppet dance (பொய்க்கரி யாட்டும் வினை), and that is grace; Pattiragiriyar's body is a puppet (பொம்மை) taken up as the exact match of the two karmas, to be thrown down before praise. The puppet moved by deed is a figure of grace in Tirumular and of bondage in Pattiragiriyar.

Sivavakkiyar tells his mind that the body is a spring of filth that rots if the salt is removed (உப்பை நீக்கில்), and asks how it can desire it; Pattiragiriyar's body is a salted pot (உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம்) that will break and take a womb again. Both make salt what keeps the body, and both set Siva's feet or rule against it.

Arunagiri's great maya is to take as 'I' a leather bag (தோற்பை) of the five elements oozing the mire of desire; Pattiragiriyar's body is a leather bag of rice (சோற்றுத் துருத்தி) carried about till he withers. Both make the body a skin bag with its contents named, and both ask to be rid of it at the Lord's feet.

Tirumular: when the breath rises the dark-smeared temple of the body becomes a gem lamp (மணிவிளக்கு); Pattiragiriyar asks to stand joined in the lamp of the sounding bell (ஓசைமணித் தீபம்), free of desire's net. The lamp lit inside the body is the goal in both; Pattiragiriyar adds sound to Tirumular's light.

Sivavakkiyar: you recite the four Vedas and do not know the foot of knowledge, like ghee hidden in milk; Pattiragiriyar asks to see the great secret the four Vedas called out for and did not see. Both leave the Vedas short of the thing itself, and neither says the Vedas are false, only that they stand outside it calling.

source_issues: 37: செஞ்சலத்தினால் திரண்ட is loosely attached and the sense is uncertain.
45: காண்டத்தை in the first line cannot be fixed with confidence.
